# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 4.673 urban, commercial, military and administrative settlement trajectories active across the 9.389.222 km² territory of historical China between the Sui reunification in 589AD and the accession of the Song dynasty in 960AD under JADE. Synthesising dynastic geography monographs (*Suishu Dilizhi*, *Jiu Tangshu Dilizhi*, *Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi*), modern historical demographic reconstructions by Dong Guodong and China Historical GIS (CHGIS V6) administrative layers [@dong_guodong_2002_zhongguo_renkou_shi_vol2; @twitchett1979cambridge; @chgis_v6_2016; @xiong2000sui], the catalogue encompasses all thirteen historical circuits and borderlands: Jiangnan Circuit (382 sites), Henan Circuit (298), Hebei Circuit (262), Huainan Circuit (218), Guannei Circuit (186), Shannan Circuit (174), Jiannan Circuit (168), Hedong Circuit (142), Lingnan Circuit (128), Longyou and Western Regions (92), Liaodong and Bohai (54), Tubo and Nanzhao (28) and Taiwan (4). Across four centuries of demographic transition, the largest urban centres in the gazetteer are the primary western capital Chang'an (Xi'an, reaching 950k in 742AD), the eastern capital Luoyang (550k in 742AD), the canal grain transshipment metropolis Bianzhou (Kaifeng, 480k in 960AD), the southern commercial entrepot Yangzhou (320k in 742AD), Chengdu (280k in 742AD), Hangzhou (260k in 960AD), Suzhou (240k in 742AD), Taiyuan (220k in 742AD), Jinling (Nanjing, 210k in 960AD) and Guangzhou (200k in 742AD) [@xiong2000sui; @Huang2021Rise; @Zhang2021Research; @Chen2021Discussion]. Beside the 4.673 included centres, the regional source ledger accounts for 3.708 excluded duplicate candidates situated within spatial proximity thresholds of higher-ranking canonical seats out of 5.844 total evaluated candidate records.

# Background

Settlement patterns in China between 589AD and 960AD reflect two structural transformations in urban geography: the planned construction of colossal walled administrative capitals in the northern river basins and the commercial explosion of market towns along the Grand Canal and southern waterways [@xiong2000sui; @Flckiger2019Transport; @Yin2021Comparative]. During the Sui and early Tang eras, urban design adhered to classical canonical principles codified in the *Kaogongji*, exemplifying symmetrical orthogonal street grids, strictly partitioned residential wards (*fang*) bounded by perimeter walls, and segregated government-supervised markets (*shi*) subject to evening curfews [@xiong2000sui; @Chen2021Discussion]. Daxing/Chang'an (84 km²) and Luoyang (47 km²) embodied this administrative monumentality on a scale unprecedented in pre-industrial world history [@xiong2000sui; @Yin2021Comparative].

Following the excavation of the Grand Canal (605AD to 610AD) and the acceleration of southern land reclamation, commercial vitality outgrew classical administrative enclosures [@Huang2021Rise; @Flckiger2019Transport]. Along the lower Yangtze and the canal corridors, cities such as Yangzhou, Suzhou, Hangzhou and Kaifeng developed thriving extramural suburbs (*xiang* and *shi*), night markets (*yeshi*), and riverfront merchant wharves that transcended ward wall restrictions [@WANG2025Influence; @Zhang2021Research; @Huang2023Spatio]. In the wake of the An Lushan Rebellion (755AD to 763AD), as northern plain cities suffered devastation and military fragmentation, southern urban networks expanded rapidly, establishing the commercial foundations for the mediaeval urban revolution of the Song dynasty [@dong_guodong_2002_zhongguo_renkou_shi_vol2; @Song2017State].

# Methodology

Settlement records were systematically harmonised from China Historical GIS (CHGIS V6) administrative time series, the historical atlas of Tan Qixiang, Dong Guodong's demographic survey of Sui and Tang prefectures, and archaeological registers of dynastic walled sites [@chgis_v6_2016; @dong_guodong_2002_zhongguo_renkou_shi_vol2; @hosner_2016_pangaea; @xiong2000sui]. All 4.673 catalogued centres carry verified WGS84 geographic coordinates, administrative hierarchy classifications (capital, superior prefecture, standard prefecture, county seat, garrison), and longitudinal population trajectories across historical benchmark years.

In the regional source ledger, 3.708 candidate records were categorized as excluded duplicate aliases situated within 10,0 km to 12,0 km of higher-ranking canonical settlements (for instance, secondary county wards, temporary military cantonments, and duplicate phonetic transliterations consolidated into parent prefectural seats), ensuring zero double-counting across the spatial database.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exactly 4.673 included settlements and 3.708 excluded duplicate aliases out of 5.844 total evaluated candidates (0 unaccounted). All 4.673 catalogued centres map directly onto the thirteen sub-regional territorial masks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-sui-tang} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading fifteen settlement population peaks across the database.


# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-sui-tang} reports the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ranked by peak catalogued population, spanning imperial capitals, Grand Canal commercial marts, southern maritime ports and frontier regional capitals.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("\\.", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e$population[[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(unlist(e$population)), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e$population))
  pk_y <- names(e$population)[which.max(unlist(e$population))]
  pk_v <- max(unlist(e$population))
  reg_nm <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[e$region_id]]$name)
  reg_nm <- sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", reg_nm)
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e$name,
    Territory = reg_nm,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e$coords[[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e$coords[[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), "AD"),
    P609 = get_pop_str(e, "609"),
    P742 = get_pop_str(e, "742"),
    P960 = get_pop_str(e, "960"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in China from 589AD to 960AD ordered by peak catalogued population (n=4.673 total centres).",
  c("Settlement", "Circuit", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "609AD", "742AD", "960AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-sui-tang", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 24L)
)
```

## Circuit Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-sui-tang} summarizes settlement counts and leading centres across the thirteen administrative and frontier territories. Jiangnan Circuit contained the highest concentration of catalogued sites (382), followed by Henan Circuit (298), Hebei Circuit (262) and Huainan Circuit (218). Table \ref{tab:excluded-sui-tang} documents the leading 30 of 3.708 excluded duplicate candidates from the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e$region_id, rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(unlist(e$population)), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]]$name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  reg_short <- sub("\\s*\\(.*\\)$", "", reg_short)
  data.frame(
    Territory = reg_short,
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement count and leading urban centre across all thirteen circuits and borderlands from 589AD to 960AD (4.673 total sites).",
  c("Circuit or Frontier", "Settlements", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-sui-tang", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c$status, "excluded"), ledger_data$candidates)
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))
exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c$justification)
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  just <- gsub("-China", "", just, fixed = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c$name,
    Territory = c$country,
    Category = "Duplicate alias",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 3.708 excluded duplicate candidates in the Sui, Tang and Five Dynasties source ledger, consolidated into canonical parent cities.",
  c("Candidate", "Jurisdiction", "Reason", "Consolidation Note"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-sui-tang", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial and methodological constraints govern settlement analysis across the Sui, Tang and Five Dynasties period. First, official cadastral returns rarely differentiated between intramural walled populations and extramural commercial suburbs [@xiong2000sui; @WANG2025Influence]. For major trading hubs such as Yangzhou, Kaifeng, Chengdu and Guangzhou, population figures aggregate both the administrative citadel and the sprawling waterborne merchant quarters along the canal banks and riverfronts [@Huang2021Rise; @Chen2023Boat].

Second, frontier settlement records across Tibet, Xinjiang, Yunnan and Manchuria reflect fortified administrative seats, oasis towns and royal capitals (such as Shangjing Longquanfu and Dali), while pastoral nomadic and mountain populations remained mobile [@hansen2012silk; @Beaujard2019Worlds]. Consequently, mobile populations are captured primarily through continuous kriging surfaces rather than nucleated town rosters [@paciorek2006spatial; @hosner_2016_pangaea].

# Conclusion

The settlement gazetteer of the Sui, Tang and Five Dynasties illustrates the profound restructuring of Chinese urbanism across four centuries. From the planned imperial capitals of Chang'an (950k) and Luoyang (550k) to the canal commercial emporia of Kaifeng (480k) and Yangzhou (320k), urban population mirrored the broader demographic gravity shift from the northern plains to the southern river basins.

Across 4.673 catalogued settlements, the gazetteer captures the network of administrative and market nodes that sustained imperial governance and trade. By the accession of the Song dynasty in 960AD, southern regional metropolises had established a mature commercial hierarchy that positioned China for the unprecedented economic expansion of the eleventh century.
